A '''Proth number''' is a [[natural number]] ''N'' of the form <math>N = k \times 2^n+1</math> where ''k'' and ''n'' are positive [[integer]]s, ''k'' is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] and <math>2^n > k</math>. A '''Proth prime''' is a Proth number that is [[Prime number|prime]]. They are named after the French mathematician [[François Proth]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite arXiv|eprint=0812.2596|title=Deterministic Primality Proving on Proth Numbers|last1=Sze|first1=Tsz-Wo|class=math.NT|year=2008}}</ref> The first few Proth primes are

:3, 5, 13, 17, 41, 97, 113, 193, 241, 257, 353, 449, 577, 641, 673, 769, 929, 1153, 1217, 1409, 1601, 2113, 2689, 2753, 3137, 3329, 3457, 4481, 4993, 6529, 7297, 7681, 7937, 9473, 9601, 9857 ({{OEIS2C|id=A080076}}).

It is still an open question whether an infinite number of Proth primes exist. It was shown in 2022 that the reciprocal sum of Proth primes converges to a real number near 0.747392479, substantially less than the value of 1.093322456 for the reciprocal sum of Proth numbers.<ref name=":proth"/>

The primality of Proth numbers can be tested more easily than many other numbers of similar magnitude.

== Definition ==
A Proth number takes the form <math>N=k \times 2^n +1</math> where ''k'' and ''n'' are positive integers, <math>k</math> is odd and <math>2^n>k</math>. A Proth prime is a Proth number that is prime.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ProthPrime.html|title=Proth Prime|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2019-12-06}}</ref> Without the condition that <math> 2^n > k</math>, all odd integers larger than 1 would be Proth numbers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/ProthNumber.html|title=Proth Number|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2019-12-07}}</ref>

== Primality testing ==
{{See also|Proth's theorem}}
The primality of a Proth number can be tested with [[Proth's theorem]], which states that a Proth number <math>p</math> is prime if and only if there exists an integer <math>a</math> for which 
:<math>a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\equiv -1 \pmod{p}.</math><ref name=":1" /><ref>{{MathWorld|title=Proth's Theorem|id=ProthsTheorem}}</ref>

This theorem can be used as a probabilistic test of primality, by checking for many random choices of <math>a</math> whether <math>a^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\equiv -1 \pmod{p}.</math>  If this fails to hold for several random <math>a</math>, then it is very likely that the number <math>p</math> is [[composite number|composite]].{{citation needed|date=December 2019}}
This test is a [[Las Vegas algorithm]]: it never returns a [[False positives and false negatives|false positive]] but can return a [[False positives and false negatives|false negative]]; in other words, it never reports a composite number as "[[Probable prime|probably prime]]" but can report a prime number as "possibly composite".

In 2008, Sze created a [[deterministic algorithm]] that runs in at most <math>\tilde{O}((k\log k+\log N)(\log N)^2)</math> time, where Õ is the [[Soft O|soft-O]] notation. For typical searches for Proth primes, usually <math>k</math> is either fixed (e.g. 321 Prime Search or Sierpinski Problem) or of order <math>O(\log N)</math> (e.g.&thinsp;[[Cullen number|Cullen prime]] search). In these cases algorithm runs in at most <math>\tilde{O}((\log N)^3)</math>, or <math>O((\log N)^{3+\epsilon})</math> time for all <math>\epsilon>0</math>. There is also an algorithm that runs in <math>\tilde{O}((\log N)^{24/7})</math> time.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|last1=Konyagin|first1=Sergei|chapter=On Primes Recognizable in Deterministic Polynomial Time|date=2013|title=The Mathematics of Paul Erdős I|pages=159–186|editor-last=Graham|editor-first=Ronald L.|editor-link=Ronald Graham|publisher=Springer New York|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-7258-2_12|isbn=978-1-4614-7258-2|last2=Pomerance|first2=Carl|editor2-last=Nešetřil|editor2-first=Jaroslav|editor3-last=Butler|editor3-first=Steve}}</ref>

Fermat numbers are a special case of Proth numbers, wherein {{math|''k''{{=}}1}}. In such a scenario [[Pépin's test]] proves that only base {{math|''a''{{=}}''3''}} need to be checked to deterministically verify or falsify the primality of a Fermat number.

== Large primes ==
{{as of|2022}}, the largest known Proth prime is <math>10223 \times 2^{31172165} + 1</math>.  It is 9,383,761 digits long.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=66|title=The Top Twenty: Proth|last=Caldwell|first=Chris|publisher=The [[Prime Pages]]}}</ref> It was found by Szabolcs Peter in the [[PrimeGrid]] volunteer computing project which announced it on 6 November 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.primegrid.com/forum_thread.php?id=7116|title=World Record Colbert Number discovered!|author=Van Zimmerman<!-- no way to tell if full name or surname-->|date=30 Nov 2016|publisher=[[PrimeGrid]]|orig-year=9 Nov 2016}}</ref> It is also the third largest known non-[[Mersenne prime]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=3|title=The Top Twenty: Largest Known Primes|last=Caldwell|first=Chris|publisher=The [[Prime Pages]]}}</ref>

The project [[Seventeen or Bust]], searching for Proth primes with a certain <math>t</math> to prove that 78557 is the smallest [[Sierpinski number]] ([[Sierpinski number#Sierpiński problem|Sierpinski problem]]), has found 11 large Proth primes by 2007. Similar resolutions to the [[Sierpinski number#Prime Sierpiński problem|prime Sierpiński problem]] and [[Sierpinski number#Extended Sierpiński problem|extended Sierpiński problem]] have yielded several more numbers.

Since divisors of [[Fermat number]]s <math>F_n = 2^{2^n} + 1</math> are always of the form <math>k \times 2^{n+2} + 1</math>, it is customary to determine if a new Proth prime divides a Fermat number.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Prime Glossary: Fermat divisor |url=https://primes.utm.edu/glossary/xpage/FermatDivisor.html |website=primes.utm.edu |access-date=14 November 2021}}</ref>

As of January 2025, [[PrimeGrid]] is the leading computing project for searching for Proth primes. Its main projects include:

* general Proth prime search
* 321 Prime Search (searching for primes of the form <math>3\times2^n+1</math>, also called [[Thabit number#Properties|Thabit primes of the second kind]])
* 27121 Prime Search (searching for primes of the form <math>27\times2^n+1</math> and <math>121\times2^n+1</math>)
* [[Cullen prime]] search (searching for primes of the form <math>n\times2^n+1</math>)
* [[Sierpinski problem]] (and their prime and extended generalizations) – searching for primes of the form <math>k \times 2^n+1</math> where ''k'' is in this list:
<blockquote>''k'' ∈ {21181, 22699, 24737, 55459, 67607, 79309, 79817, 91549, 99739, 131179, 152267, 156511, 163187, 200749, 209611, 222113, 225931, 227723, 229673, 237019, 238411}</blockquote>

As of June 2023, the largest Proth primes discovered are:<ref name="top20">{{Cite web|url=https://primes.utm.edu/top20/page.php?id=66|title=The top twenty: Proth|last=Caldwell|first=Chris K.|website=The Top Twenty|access-date=6 December 2019}}</ref>

== Proth prime of the second kind ==

A '''Proth number of the second kind''' is a [[natural number]] ''N'' of the form <math>N = k \times 2^n-1</math> where ''k'' and ''n'' are positive [[integer]]s, ''k'' is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] and <math>2^n > k</math>. A '''Proth prime of the second kind''' is a Proth number of the second kind that is [[Prime number|prime]]. The first few Proth primes of the second kind are

:3, 7, 11, 23, 31, 47, 79, 127, 191, 223, 239, 383, 479, 607, 863, 991, 1087, 1151, 1279, 1471, 1663, 2111, 2239, 2687, 2879, 3391, 3583, 3967, 5119, 5503, 6143, 6271, 6911, 7039, 8191, 8447, 8831, 9343 ({{OEIS2C|id=A112715}}).

The largest Proth primes of the second kind can be primality testing use the [[Lucas–Lehmer–Riesel test]].

As of January 2025, [[PrimeGrid]] is the leading computing project for searching for Proth primes of the second kind. Its main projects include:

* general Proth prime of the second kind search
* 321 Prime Search (searching for primes of the form <math>3\times2^n-1</math>, also called [[Thabit prime]]s)
* 27121 Prime Search (searching for primes of the form <math>27\times2^n-1</math> and <math>121\times2^n-1</math>)
* [[Woodall prime]] search (searching for primes of the form <math>n\times2^n-1</math>)
* [[Riesel problem]] (and their prime and extended generalizations) – searching for primes of the form <math>k \times 2^n-1</math> where ''k'' is in this list:
<blockquote>''k'' ∈ {23669, 31859, 38473, 46663, 67117, 74699, 81041, 121889, 129007, 143047, 161669, 206231, 215443, 226153, 234343, 245561, 250027, 315929, 319511, 324011, 325123, 327671, 336839, 342847, 344759, 362609, 363343, 364903, 365159, 368411, 371893, 384539, 386801, 397027, 409753, 444637, 470173, 474491, 477583, 485557, 494743 }</blockquote>

== Uses ==
Small Proth primes (less than 10<sup>200</sup>) have been used in constructing prime ladders, sequences of prime numbers such that each term is "close" (within about 10<sup>11</sup>) to the previous one.  Such ladders have been used to empirically verify prime-related [[conjecture]]s.  For example, [[Goldbach's weak conjecture]] was verified in 2008 up to 8.875 × 10<sup>30</sup> using prime ladders constructed from Proth primes.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=1305.3062|title=Numerical Verification of the Ternary Goldbach Conjecture up to 8.875e30|last1=Helfgott|first1=H. A.|last2=Platt|first2=David J.|class=math.NT|year=2013}}</ref>  (The conjecture was later proved by [[Harald Helfgott]].<ref name=":02">{{cite arXiv|eprint=1312.7748|class=math.NT|first=Harald A.|last=Helfgott|title=The ternary Goldbach conjecture is true|year=2013}}</ref><ref name="humboldt-professur.de">{{Cite news|url=https://www.humboldt-professur.de/en/preistraeger/preistraeger-2015/helfgott-harald-andres|title=Harald Andrés Helfgott|website=Alexander von Humboldt-Professur|access-date=2019-12-08}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=December 2019}})

Also, Proth primes can optimize [[den Boer reduction]] between the [[Diffie–Hellman problem]] and the [[Discrete logarithm|Discrete logarithm problem]]. The prime number 55 × 2<sup>286</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 has been used in this way.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Brown|first=Daniel R. L.|date=24 Feb 2015|title=CM55: special prime-field elliptic curves almost optimizing den Boer's reduction between Diffie–Hellman and discrete logs|url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2014/877.pdf|journal=International Association for Cryptologic Research|pages=1–3}}</ref>

As Proth primes have simple [[binary number|binary]] representations, they have also been used in fast modular reduction without the need for pre-computation, for example by [[Microsoft]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Acar|first1=Tolga|last2=Shumow|first2=Dan|date=2010|title=Modular Reduction without Pre-Computation for Special Moduli|url=https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/modmul_no_precomp.pdf|journal=Microsoft Research}}</ref>
